blocks.md:
A short poem written for this lesson.

*The river is a silver snake,
it slides through the green hills.
The sun is a golden coin
that the sky has lent to us.
The wind whispers to the trees,
and the trees dance slowly.*

blocks.title: Pictures with words
blocks.md: A **simile** compares two things using *like* or *as*: *as busy as a bee*. A **metaphor** says that one thing **is** another: *The river is a silver snake.* **Personification** gives a thing the actions of a person: *The wind whispers.* These make a poem more colourful. A **stanza** is a group of lines.

items.text: The sun is a golden coin.

blocks.caption: Three poetic devices.
blocks.alt: A table of devices: simile with the example as busy as a bee; metaphor with the sun is a golden coin; personification with the wind whispered.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- Saying that a metaphor uses *like* or *as*: that is a simile.
- Thinking that a poem must always rhyme: many poems do not.
- Retelling the poem line by line instead of saying what it makes you feel and see.
- Reading too fast, without pauses.

blocks.title: Example 1
blocks.statement: Is 'The sun is a golden coin' a simile or a metaphor?
steps: It says the sun is a coin, without like or as.

blocks.title: Example 2
blocks.statement: Find the personification in the poem.
steps: Look for a thing that does what a person does.
The wind whispers to the trees (and the trees dance).
blocks.answer: The wind whispers to the trees.

lessons.title: Oral English: stress, intonation and conversation
lessons.programRef: MINEDUB primary school curriculum (English-speaking subsystem), Level III (Class 5) — English Language; to be checked against the official syllabus
lessons.author: CastBridge (AI draft)
lessons.source: Original writing following the Cameroonian curriculum; to be reviewed by a teacher
objectives: Say words with the stress in the right place.
Use a rising tone for questions and a falling tone for statements.
Take part in a polite conversation.
reviewNotes: Stress patterns follow standard British models; Cameroon English differs in places; a teacher should adapt it. Audio is not included.
Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.title: Word stress
blocks.md: In a word with more than one syllable, one syllable is said **louder and longer**: *TEAcher, aBOUT, CAMeroon, deCIDE*. Listen to the stressed syllable and repeat. Putting the stress in the wrong place can make a word hard to understand. A dictionary shows the stress with a mark.

blocks.caption: Words with the stressed part in capitals.
blocks.alt: A table of words and the place of the stress: teacher, first; about, second; Cameroon, first; decide, second; welcome, first.

blocks.title: Intonation
blocks.md: The **voice goes up** at the end of a yes/no question (*Are you ready?*) and **goes down** at the end of a statement (*I am ready.*) and a question with *who, what, where* (*Where do you live?*). In a list, the voice goes up on each item and down on the last: *rice, beans, oil and salt.*

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- Saying every syllable with the same strength.
- Using a flat voice for questions.
- Not looking at the listener.
- Talking too fast: speak clearly and listen to each other.

blocks.title: Example 1
steps: The stress is on the second syllable.

blocks.title: Example 2
blocks.statement: Does the voice go up or down at the end of 'Are you hungry?'

exercises.source: Original exercise written for CastBridge, in the style of the curriculum
exercises.prompt: Write a short dialogue (6 lines) between two pupils meeting on the first day of the term. Include a greeting, a question, an answer and polite words.
exercises.model:
Ako: Good morning, Bih! How are you?
Bih: I am fine, thank you. And you?
Ako: I am very well. Did you have a good holiday?
Bih: Yes, I visited my grandmother in Bamenda. What about you?
Ako: I stayed in Buea. Shall we sit together?
Bih: Yes, please. Let us find a desk.
exercises.rubric: Marks (6): greeting (1); questions and answers (2); polite words (1); at least six lines in the right order (1); punctuation and speech layout (1).
